Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Demo: Redwood for embeddings + reranking (Apex Retail Search)
Date: 2026-01-08
Time: 11:03 AM - 11:45 AM PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Priyom Das (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Sales Engineering)
- Jordan Kim (Apex Retail, Search Eng Manager)
- Maya Desai (Apex Retail, ML Engineer)
- Chris O’Neill (Apex Retail, Platform/SRE)
- Elena Park (Apex Retail, Product - Search)

---
Auto Summary (generated)
- Redwood walked through an embeddings + reranking workflow tailored to Apex’s retail search use case.
- Demo included request-level cost/latency breakdown in Console, plus how caching and batching reduce unit cost.
- Apex asked about rerank latency at higher candidate counts, observability exports, and whether caching is deterministic/safe.
- Next steps include sharing code snippets, collecting Apex workload stats, and scheduling a deeper technical session.

Topics
- Embeddings endpoint + model pinning
- Reranking endpoint (top-K candidates) and latency expectations
- Console observability: per-route latency, cost per request, token breakdown, errors
- Caching/batching toggles and “where the savings come from”
- Deployment options (hosted now; VPC/private later)

Questions captured
- Does Redwood cache embeddings by default or is it opt-in?
- How does rerank cost scale with candidate count (50 vs 200)?
- Can we export traces to Datadog / OpenTelemetry?
- If a model version changes in the catalog, can we pin for stability?
- What’s the failure mode if a region is out of capacity during peak?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Priyom Das: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. Um, today we’re gonna do a quick run through focused on embeddings and reranking for search, and then we’ll spend a few minutes in the Console so you can see how we break down cost and latency.

[00:13] Jordan Kim: Sounds good.

[00:14] Markus Klein: Hey all.

[00:16] Elena Park: Hi.

[00:17] Priyom Das: Before we jump in, Jordan, quick check—are you mainly thinking site search, like query to product catalog, or also recs, like “similar items”?

[00:27] Jordan Kim: Both. Search is the big one. We have a vector retrieval piece today and we’re experimenting with rerank. Recs is next.

[00:34] Maya Desai: Yeah and we’re evaluating whether we can unify across those, instead of like, one vendor for embed and another for rerank.

[00:41] Priyom Das: Perfect. That’s basically the story we’ll tell: unified inference endpoints, consistent ops, plus knobs for economics.

[00:47] Chris O’Neill: And observability. That’s been a pain. Like, we get a bill and then no one can map it to routes.

[00:53] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll show that.

[00:55] Priyom Das: Okay. Markus is driving the live demo. If anything’s unclear, stop us.

[01:01] Markus Klein: Alright, sharing screen… you should see Redwood Console.

[01:04] Maya Desai: Yep.

[01:06] Markus Klein: Cool. This is our demo tenant, but the layout matches prod. On the left is Projects, routes, models. For Apex, imagine you have “search-prod” and “recs-prod” as separate projects. Today I’ll use “apex-search-demo”.

[01:21] Markus Klein: First piece: embeddings. The API is basically: /v1/embeddings. We support a few embedding model families. For the demo we’ve pinned to a specific version, so we don’t get surprises if the catalog updates.

[01:33] Jordan Kim: When you say pinned, like exact model hash?

[01:36] Markus Klein: Yeah, exact model version ID. You can also pin by “family + version”, but for enterprise workflows we recommend exact pin.

[01:43] Chris O’Neill: And who controls that? Us or you?

[01:45] Markus Klein: You control it per route. You can do staged rollouts, canary, A/B. We’ll show that view later, but we’ll keep it simple today.

[01:55] Priyom Das: Also, we’ve built this whole demo environment specifically so the model pin doesn’t move under you. Just calling that out—this is a common demo failure mode.

[02:03] Elena Park: Appreciated.

[02:05] Markus Klein: So here’s a tiny script. I’ll run a query embedding for “waterproof hiking boots size 10”.

[02:12] (keyboard sounds)

[02:16] Markus Klein: Response comes back with the vector, and we return metadata like model, dimension, and usage. We track usage as “embedding units” on the billing side, but inside Console you can see per-request cost.

[02:27] Maya Desai: Is it token-based under the hood or like per call?

[02:30] Markus Klein: It’s model dependent. Some are token-like, but we normalize into embedding units so pricing stays stable. The Console will still show you the payload size and time.

[02:41] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[02:43] Markus Klein: Next is rerank. Flow is usually: query embedding -> retrieve top N from vector DB -> call rerank model with query + candidates -> rerank scores.

[02:55] Maya Desai: We use Pinecone right now.

[02:57] Markus Klein: Totally fine. We’re not trying to replace Pinecone or Weaviate. We sit on the inference side.

[03:03] Priyom Das: Yeah, we partner with those teams pretty often.

[03:06] Markus Klein: Let me run rerank with… I’ll do top 50 candidates. Here’s a set of product titles and short descriptions. Calling /v1/rerank.

[03:16] (keyboard)

[03:19] Markus Klein: Okay, response. You see scores, ordered list, and we also return usage tokens for the rerank model.

[03:26] Jordan Kim: What’s the typical latency on rerank? Like p95.

[03:30] Markus Klein: It depends on candidate count and text length, but for 50 short candidates we usually see tens of milliseconds to low hundreds, depending on region and load. In a dedicated pool you can get tighter predictability.

[03:44] Chris O’Neill: That’s the thing—predictability. We got burned with shared endpoints.

[03:49] Priyom Das: Yeah, so we have hosted and then dedicated capacity. For today we’re on a hosted-like environment but we’ll show the controls and how you can reason about it. If you need strict QPS and SLOs, dedicated is usually the next step.

[04:04] Elena Park: For search, we have a pretty strict p95. Like, overall page p95 is 300ms, so rerank can’t be 500.

[04:11] Markus Klein: Totally. A common pattern: retrieve top 200, but only rerank top 50. Or do a two-stage rerank with a cheaper model then a heavier one.

[04:23] Maya Desai: How does cost scale with candidates? It’s basically query + each candidate, right?

[04:27] Markus Klein: Exactly. The rerank model sees query plus each candidate. So candidate count is the biggest lever. That’s why in Console we show token breakdown on rerank routes.

[04:38] Priyom Das: This is where “production economics” comes in. Not just “here’s a model”, but “what knobs move your spend without guessing.”

[04:46] Markus Klein: Let’s jump into observability. In Console, I’ll go to Routes -> “apex-search-rerank”.

[04:54] Markus Klein: You’ll see latency distribution, error rate, and cost per request. This demo tenant has synthetic traffic running so it’s not empty.

[05:03] Chris O’Neill: Thank you. We’ve had so many vendor demos where dashboards are blank.

[05:07] Markus Klein: Yeah, we seed it. Okay so here: p50 is ~85ms, p95 ~160ms, last 24 hours. Errors basically zero.

[05:17] Maya Desai: And the cost per request is… where is that number coming from.

[05:20] Markus Klein: Click “Cost breakdown”.

[05:22] (click)

[05:24] Markus Klein: So this is token-level cost. You see prompt tokens (query + candidates), completion tokens (for rerank it’s mostly scoring, so not a long generation), and then overhead. We separate compute time, queue time, and network.

[05:38] Jordan Kim: Queue time is interesting. That’s basically batching?

[05:41] Markus Klein: Queue time is mostly waiting for batching or GPU availability. Batching is a double-edged sword: it increases throughput and reduces cost, but can add some queue latency.

[05:51] Chris O’Neill: Can we control that?

[05:53] Markus Klein: Yep. Per route, you can set batching policy. For rerank you often want small batch windows. For embeddings you can batch more aggressively.

[06:04] Maya Desai: Is caching an option? Like if the same query repeats.

[06:08] Markus Klein: Yes. There are two caching stories. For generative chat we do prefix/KV caching. For embeddings, we can do request-result caching at the route layer—if the exact input repeats, you can hit cache.

[06:22] Jordan Kim: Is that on by default?

[06:24] Markus Klein: Not by default for most customers, because people have opinions on correctness and privacy. But for search queries, if you’re okay with it, it can be a big win.

[06:34] Priyom Das: We usually recommend starting with caching in a bounded way: TTL, max size, and only for routes that are safe.

[06:40] Chris O’Neill: And it shows up in cost savings clearly?

[06:43] Markus Klein: Yep. Let me show you. I’m going to flip to the embeddings route “apex-search-embed”. Here’s a panel called “Cache hit rate”.

[06:52] Markus Klein: You see about 32% hit rate in the synthetic workload. And then you see the effective cost per request drop because cache hits are basically near-zero compute.

[07:04] Maya Desai: Okay, so it’s not like the model is faster; you’re skipping work.

[07:07] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[07:09] Jordan Kim: Our queries repeat, but not exact strings always. Like “boots waterproof” vs “waterproof boots”.

[07:14] Markus Klein: Yeah, exact-match caching won’t catch that. Some customers do canonicalization upstream. But for embeddings, you can also cache on normalized query strings.

[07:24] Chris O’Neill: One worry: if we cache, do we leak across tenants?

[07:28] Markus Klein: No, cache is per project/route. Isolation boundaries apply.

[07:33] Priyom Das: Also, you can choose dedicated capacity if isolation is a bigger concern.

[07:38] Elena Park: I’m curious how you’d message this to leadership. Like, “we can save X.” Do you have examples?

[07:44] Priyom Das: We can share ranges and the levers: candidate count, batching, cache hit rate. We avoid promising a single number without workload data, but we can do a quick model.

[07:55] Markus Klein: Let me run a side-by-side. I’ll trigger rerank with top 200 candidates so you see how tokens move.

[08:03] (keyboard)

[08:07] Markus Klein: Okay rerank(200). You’ll see latency bumped to ~240ms p95 for this run, and cost per request roughly quadrupled because tokens scale linearly-ish with candidate count.

[08:20] Maya Desai: That aligns with our expectation.

[08:22] Jordan Kim: Is there any trick to make rerank(200) cheaper besides just… not doing it.

[08:27] Markus Klein: Mostly reduce text length per candidate (title only, or truncated description), reduce candidate count, or use a smaller rerank model. Quantization can help too depending on the model.

[08:39] Chris O’Neill: Quantization… do you offer that or is that us.

[08:42] Markus Klein: We offer profiles. You choose “balanced” or “cost-optimized”, and we’ll pick kernels / quantization settings that are safe for quality. If you want full control, that’s more like Private deployment.

[08:56] Priyom Das: But for search, we typically validate with an eval set so we’re not guessing on quality.

[09:01] Maya Desai: We have offline metrics. NDCG, MRR, that kind of thing.

[09:05] Markus Klein: Great. We can integrate that. We have prompt sets and evals in Console, but for embeddings/rerank it’s more like a dataset run.

[09:14] Jordan Kim: Can you show traces? Like per request.

[09:17] Markus Klein: Yeah. Going to “Traces”. Here’s a request trace for rerank. You see: auth, routing, queue, model execution, response.

[09:27] Chris O’Neill: Can we export that to Datadog.

[09:30] Markus Klein: We support OpenTelemetry export. Datadog, Honeycomb, whatever. Some fields might be limited in hosted vs private, but you can get request IDs, latencies, and error codes.

[09:43] Maya Desai: Do you log the full payload? Because that’s sensitive.

[09:47] Markus Klein: Good question. By default, we don’t log full prompts/payloads in plaintext. You can enable sampling with redaction, and for strict environments it’s Private with customer-managed logging.

[09:58] Priyom Das: We can send our security FAQ after the call. It’s got the short answers: retention, audit logs, encryption.

[10:04] Elena Park: Please.

[10:06] Markus Klein: On the cost breakdown: you can slice by route, by model, by key, and by environment. So if your mobile team is using embeddings for recs, you can tag that separately.

[10:18] Jordan Kim: Tags like headers?

[10:20] Markus Klein: Yep, metadata tags. Or separate API keys per service.

[10:26] Chris O’Neill: That’s probably what we’d do. Separate keys.

[10:30] Priyom Das: And those keys can be scoped least-privilege. Like only embeddings, only rerank.

[10:37] Maya Desai: Okay.

[10:38] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick “caching wins” view. This chart shows cost per 1k requests over time with cache hit rate overlay. When hit rate increases, the cost line drops.

[10:53] Jordan Kim: How are you generating that hit rate here? Synthetic.

[10:56] Markus Klein: Yeah, synthetic workload simulates diurnal patterns and repeated head queries.

[11:02] Elena Park: Our head queries are crazy concentrated, so caching might be huge.

[11:06] Maya Desai: But we also have personalization. Like logged-in user context.

[11:09] Markus Klein: If the embed input includes user context, caching becomes less effective. But for general query embeddings it’s still good.

[11:17] Chris O’Neill: Do you support “private cache” per key.

[11:20] Markus Klein: Per route, per project, per org. Per key is possible but not the default knob. We can talk about it if needed.

[11:30] Priyom Das: Usually the isolation boundary is tenant/project. For personalization, you can keep caching off and lean on batching.

[11:38] Jordan Kim: Can you explain batching again? Like, are you batching across customers? That’s the noisy neighbor problem.

[11:44] Markus Klein: In hosted, yes there’s shared infrastructure, but we isolate by quotas and scheduling. In dedicated, batching is within your reserved pool.

[11:54] Chris O’Neill: So if we need guarantees, dedicated.

[11:56] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[12:00] Priyom Das: And dedicated is not “here’s a cluster you run.” It’s still the same API and Console, just dedicated capacity.

[12:07] Elena Park: Can we start hosted and then move.

[12:09] Priyom Das: Yes, that’s common. Start hosted for quick integration. When usage or requirements justify it, switch the route to dedicated pool.

[12:18] Jordan Kim: We’re also considering Bedrock for some of this.

[12:22] Priyom Das: Totally fair. Bedrock is great if you want everything inside AWS accounts and you’re okay with those operational surfaces. Where we win is more control over serving economics and consistent tooling across hosted/dedicated/private.

[12:35] Maya Desai: And you support open models.

[12:37] Markus Klein: Yeah. You can pick model families and we optimize runtime. We’re not tied to a single provider.

[12:43] Chris O’Neill: What about region. We need us-east and maybe eu-west later.

[12:47] Markus Klein: Hosted we have multiple regions. Dedicated is region-specific. For Private you can do VPC and choose your cloud.

[12:55] Priyom Das: For today’s demo we’re in us-west, but we can run a latency test in us-east once we know your user distribution.

[13:03] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[13:05] Markus Klein: I’ll show errors and retries quickly. Here’s a synthetic error injection (timeout) and how the client can retry with idempotency keys.

[13:14] Maya Desai: That’s more for chat.

[13:16] Markus Klein: True, but even for embeddings if you do bulk jobs, retries matter.

[13:21] Chris O’Neill: We do nightly re-embed.

[13:23] Markus Klein: Exactly. And there you might prefer higher throughput and bigger batch windows.

[13:30] Priyom Das: Maya, can I ask what throughput you’re targeting? Like QPS peak.

[13:35] Maya Desai: Search is like… peak 800 QPS on weekends. Embedding is mostly offline. Rerank would be online.

[13:43] Jordan Kim: But not all queries rerank. It’s maybe 30%.

[13:47] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. For 240 rerank QPS, we can size dedicated pretty precisely.

[13:54] Chris O’Neill: And price? Like, how does it compare to OpenAI embeddings.

[13:58] Priyom Das: We can follow up with a detailed pricing sheet. It’ll come down to model choice and caching. But the core message: we give you visibility so you can tune. If you’re just comparing list price per 1k tokens, it’s incomplete.

[14:12] Elena Park: Leadership will compare list prices anyway.

[14:15] Priyom Das: Totally. We’ll arm you with both: list price and effective price after batching/caching.

[14:22] Markus Klein: Also if you care about rerank quality, you might choose a model that’s slightly more expensive but requires fewer candidates. That can reduce total cost.

[14:34] Maya Desai: That’s interesting actually.

[14:37] Jordan Kim: Can you show me where you see candidate count in the dashboard.

[14:41] Markus Klein: We capture input sizes. Here in “Request attributes”, you see number of documents, average tokens per doc, query length.

[14:50] Chris O’Neill: That’s gold.

[14:52] Markus Klein: It helps you catch regressions, like someone starts sending full HTML product pages.

[15:00] Jordan Kim: (laughs) yeah, that happens.

[15:03] Priyom Das: We’ve seen it.

[15:05] Markus Klein: Okay, last piece: rollouts. Not sure if you need it for embeddings/rerank, but if you want to test a new embedding model, you can do A/B.

[15:14] Maya Desai: We do that offline mostly.

[15:16] Markus Klein: Right. But if you want to do shadow traffic, you can route 5% to new model and compare metrics.

[15:24] Chris O’Neill: Does that double cost.

[15:26] Markus Klein: It can, because you’re running extra inference. Some customers only shadow a small percentage or only for certain cohorts.

[15:35] Priyom Das: Or do it in batch offline.

[15:38] Elena Park: For POC we’d probably do offline first.

[15:41] Priyom Das: Makes sense.

[15:43] Markus Klein: I’ll stop sharing in a sec. Any other questions.

[15:47] Jordan Kim: Yeah—caching. For embeddings caching, do you store the raw text.

[15:52] Markus Klein: We store a hash key and the resulting embedding vector. Implementation details depend on deployment mode. In hosted, it’s within your tenant boundary. You can configure TTL and can disable caching entirely.

[16:06] Maya Desai: Okay. And rerank caching? Is that a thing.

[16:10] Markus Klein: Technically you can cache rerank responses too, but because candidates change and personalization, it’s less common.

[16:17] Chris O’Neill: Observability export—you said OTel. Is there sampling.

[16:22] Markus Klein: Yes, configurable sampling. For high QPS you don’t want 100% traces.

[16:27] Priyom Das: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[16:31] Priyom Das: We showed embeddings, rerank, and how Console shows you token/cost breakdown, plus cache hit rate. Next, Markus can send you code snippets for the pipeline, and if you can share your distribution—candidate count, lengths, QPS—we can recommend batching/caching defaults and whether hosted is enough or dedicated makes sense.

[16:52] Jordan Kim: Yep. We can do that.

[16:54] Maya Desai: I’d also like the model names / versions you used.

[16:57] Markus Klein: Yep, I’ll email those. And a link to the example app.

[17:01] Chris O’Neill: And security docs.

[17:03] Priyom Das: I’ll send the security FAQ link and a short summary. If we need a deeper security call, we can pull in our security advisor, but maybe we wait until after we align on POC scope.

[17:15] Elena Park: Works.

[17:17] Priyom Das: Great. Thanks everyone.

[17:20] Jordan Kim: Thanks.

[17:21] Maya Desai: Thank you.

[17:22] Chris O’Neill: Thanks.

---
Notes
- Some portions of the transcript may contain minor inaccuracies due to audio quality and overlapping speech.
- Links referenced (to be sent in follow-up): demo repo, model/version IDs, security FAQ, and pricing guidance.
